title: The Little Shop of Horrors

This is a secondary source only. No primary notice-failure record or Catalog of Copyright Entries search was fetched in this session, so the print is not marked verified.

evidence.note: The title is used by a licensed stage-musical franchise. Avoid using it as branding for products or shows. No trademark registration was checked.

A faithful restoration of a public-domain film adds no new US copyright: copying or restoring public-domain images without original creative additions is not protected (Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp., S.D.N.Y. 1999, following Feist v. Rural, 1991). What a restoration ADDS can be protected: a newly composed or newly recorded score, colorization, newly written or translated titles and subtitles, and other original additions. Separately, ripping a copy-protected Blu-ray or DVD can break the DMCA's anti-circumvention rule (17 U.S.C. 1201) even when the film itself is public domain.
evidence.source: Bridgeman Art Library v. Corel Corp. (summary)

evidence.note: 17 U.S.C. 1201 - circumvention of copyright protection systems.
Colorized versions and modern restorations are separately protected.

editorial:
Roger Corman's The Little Shop of Horrors, released September 14, 1960 by The Filmgroup and Santa Clara Productions, was written by Charles B. Griffith, whose screenplay was initially titled The Passionate People Eater. Its music is credited to cellist Fred Katz, written originally for A Bucket of Blood, with additional uncredited music by Ronald Stein. Wikipedia reports that Corman did not believe it had much financial prospect after its initial theatrical run and did not bother to copyright it. That account is secondary, and no primary record has been attached here.

The rights trap is the franchise built on top of it. The 1982 stage musical and the 1986 film are separate derivative works, so their songs and book are not covered by the 1960 film's status. The title is also used by a licensed musical franchise, so avoid it as branding. Treat the print as likely free but unverified until a primary record is attached.
faq: Can I use the songs from Little Shop of Horrors?
Not on the strength of the 1960 film. The songs come from the 1982 musical and 1986 film, which are separate derivative works. They are not covered by anything said here about the 1960 original.

The 1960 film is widely reported to have entered the public domain through failure to copyright, but this dossier has no primary record, so the print stays Undetermined. If you rely on it, keep your own evidence. Do not assume that any particular restored copy or added score is free.
